questions.title: Fourth arch cartilage and the thyroid cartilage
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the branchial (pharyngeal) arches is CORRECT?

options.A: The cartilage of the third arch gives origin to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone
options.B: The cartilage of the fifth arch gives origin to the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages
options.C: The ventral portions of the cartilages of the fourth arch forms the thyroid cartilage
options.D: The stapes arises in the upper part of the third arch

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lesser cornu and upper part of the body of the hyoid bone derive from the second (hyoid) arch cartilage, not the third; the third arch cartilage instead forms the greater cornu and lower part of the hyoid body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no persisting fifth pharyngeal arch cartilage in humans — the fifth arch is transient and leaves no skeletal derivative; the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages instead derive from the sixth arch cartilage.
explanations.C: Correct. The laryngeal cartilages develop from the fourth and sixth arch cartilage bars, and specifically the paired ventral portions of the fourth arch cartilage fuse in the midline to form the thyroid cartilage. This is a key exception students must memorise arch-by-arch, since the fourth and sixth arches (not the more commonly cited first three) supply the larynx. Recognising this lets you correctly separate thyroid cartilage (fourth arch) from cricoid/arytenoid/corniculate cartilage (sixth arch).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The stapes arises from the second (hyoid) pharyngeal arch cartilage, not the third; the third arch cartilage contributes only to the hyoid bone, not to any middle-ear ossicle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fourth pharyngeal arch cartilage's ventral portion forms the thyroid cartilage, and that no fifth-arch cartilage persists.

questions.title: Second pharyngeal arch muscular derivative
questions.question: The branchial arches (or pharyngeal arches) develop during the fourth and fifth week in utero as a series of mesodermal outpouchings on either side of the developing pharynx. The second pharyngeal arch gives rise to the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior belly of digastric is a first-arch derivative, innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), not the second arch's facial nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stylopharyngeus is a third-arch derivative, innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which is the defining nerve of the third arch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Geniohyoid is not a pharyngeal arch muscle at all; it develops from the occipital myotomes and is innervated by fibers of C1 riding on the hypoglossal nerve.
explanations.D: Correct. Stylohyoid is a second (hyoid) arch derivative, along with the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, and the posterior belly of digastric, all sharing the second arch's nerve, the facial nerve (CN VII). This muscle-by-muscle, arch-by-arch, nerve-by-nerve pattern is the organising principle the exam is testing — each arch's muscles share one cranial nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify stylohyoid as a second (facial-nerve) pharyngeal arch muscle, distinct from first- and third-arch muscles and non-arch geniohyoid.

questions.title: The vascular layer of the scalp
questions.question: Which of the following layers is considered the vascular layer of the scalp?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Skin is the outermost layer, containing hair follicles and sebaceous glands, but the scalp's named vessels run in the layer beneath it, not within the skin itself.
explanations.B: Correct. The dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer — the second layer in the SCALP mnemonic (Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium) — carries the scalp's arteries and cutaneous nerves, tethered by fibrous septa to the skin above and the aponeurosis below. This tethering is also why lacerations here bleed profusely: the vessels cannot retract into the fibrous tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) is a tough, tendinous, relatively avascular sheet connecting the occipitofrontalis muscle bellies, not the vascular layer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The loose areolar tissue layer is the 'danger area' of the scalp because infection spreads easily through it into emissary veins, but it is not itself the named vascular layer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the dense connective tissue layer, not the aponeurosis, as the vascular layer of the scalp within the SCALP scheme.

questions.title: Preganglionic parasympathetic pathway to the lacrimal gland
questions.question: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland run in which nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The chorda tympani is also a facial-nerve parasympathetic branch, but it supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands (via the submandibular ganglion), not the lacrimal gland.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zygomaticotemporal nerve is a sensory branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) that carries the lacrimal gland's postganglionic secretomotor fibers only as a communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve; it is not the preganglionic parasympathetic pathway itself.
explanations.C: Correct. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland arise in the superior salivatory nucleus and leave the facial nerve as the greater petrosal nerve. This joins the deep petrosal (sympathetic) nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal and reaches the pterygopalatine ganglion, where the parasympathetic fibers synapse. Postganglionic fibers then travel via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves onward to the gland itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the otic ganglion, supplying the parotid gland, not the lacrimal gland.

questions.learning_objective: Trace preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland through the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, distinct from the chorda tympani route.

questions.title: The suprathalamic caudate
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a suprathalamic structure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tail of the caudate curves inferiorly around the thalamus into the roof of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, ending near the amygdala — it sits lateral/inferior to the thalamus, not directly above it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The head of the caudate lies anterolateral to the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle, rostral to the thalamus, not directly superior to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) lies lateral to the thalamus, separated from it by the internal capsule, not above it.
explanations.D: Correct. The body of the caudate nucleus runs along the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle, directly superior to the thalamus, separated from it by the stria terminalis and thalamostriate vein. This is why the body specifically, and not the whole caudate, is described as a suprathalamic structure — a useful landmark when reading axial MRI at the level of the thalamus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the body of the caudate nucleus as the suprathalamic part of the caudate, distinguishing it from the head, tail and lentiform nucleus.

questions.title: Vagus nerve course in the carotid sheath
questions.question: Which of the following nerve passes between internal jugular vein and common carotid artery?

explanations.A: Correct. Within the carotid sheath, the vagus nerve (CN X) descends in the posterior groove between the internal jugular vein (laterally) and the internal/common carotid artery (medially), a constant relationship used surgically to identify it. This anatomical constant is also why carotid sheath dissections and central line placement are taught with the vein lateral and the artery medial to the nerve in between.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) crosses superficial to both the internal and external carotid arteries on its way to the tongue, but it does not run within the carotid sheath in the groove between vein and artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the internal and external carotid arteries more superiorly in the neck, not between the jugular vein and the carotid artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The accessory nerve (CN XI) exits the carotid sheath early, crossing the internal jugular vein to reach the posterior triangle and sternocleidomastoid, rather than running within the sheath alongside the vagus.

questions.subtopic: Vagus nerve course in the neck
questions.learning_objective: Locate the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery.

questions.title: Ansa cervicalis and the omohyoid muscle
questions.question: The ansa cervicalis supplies one of the following muscles:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mylohyoid is a first-arch muscle supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), not the ansa cervicalis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stylohyoid is a second-arch muscle supplied directly by the facial nerve (CN VII), unrelated to the cervical plexus loop.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyrohyoid, despite being an infrahyoid ('strap') muscle like the ansa-supplied group, is supplied directly by C1 fibers that travel on the hypoglossal nerve, bypassing the ansa cervicalis loop entirely.
explanations.D: Correct. The ansa cervicalis, a loop of the cervical plexus formed by a superior root (C1 fibers on the hypoglossal nerve) and inferior root (C2-C3), supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. These strap muscles fix the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech, which is why ansa cervicalis injury can subtly affect laryngeal positioning.

questions.learning_objective: Identify omohyoid as an ansa-cervicalis-innervated infrahyoid muscle, distinct from thyrohyoid's direct C1/hypoglossal supply.

questions.title: Abducens nerve within the cavernous sinus
questions.question: Which of the following nerves run in the cavity of cavernous sinus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mandibular nerve (V3) exits the skull through foramen ovale without traversing the cavernous sinus; only the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve run in the sinus's lateral wall.
explanations.B: Correct. The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique among the nerves related to the cavernous sinus in running freely within the venous cavity itself, immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery, rather than within the sinus's lateral dural wall — which is why it is the cranial nerve most vulnerable to compression from cavernous sinus pathology (e.g. thrombosis, carotid-cavernous fistula, pituitary tumour).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The optic nerve (CN II) lies superior to the cavernous sinus, related to it only via the optic canal and chiasm, not within the sinus itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, embedded in dura, rather than freely within the venous cavity like the abducens nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the abducens nerve as the cranial nerve running freely within the cavernous sinus cavity itself.

questions.title: The tectum as dorsal midbrain
questions.question: tectum is a part of which of the following structure?

explanations.A: Correct. The tectum ('roof') is the dorsal part of the midbrain, formed by the superior and inferior colliculi (corpora quadrigemina), which mediate visual and auditory reflexes respectively. The superior colliculi drive saccadic eye movements toward a visual stimulus, while the inferior colliculi relay auditory information toward the medial geniculate body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pons is a separate brainstem subdivision caudal to the midbrain, containing its own nuclei (e.g. pontine nuclei, abducens nucleus) but no tectum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus) lies immediately rostral to the midbrain; the tectum is midbrain tissue, not diencephalic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medulla oblongata is the most caudal brainstem subdivision, containing the pyramids and olives, with no tectum of its own.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the tectum as the dorsal midbrain, formed by the superior and inferior colliculi.

questions.title: The broadest, deepest cortical layer
questions.question: what is the broadest and deepest layer in the cerebral cortex?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The plexiform (molecular) layer is layer I, the most superficial and one of the thinnest layers, at the opposite end of the six-layer stack from the deepest layer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal granular layer is layer IV, a mid-depth layer that is the principal thalamic input layer, not the deepest or broadest.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The layer containing giant pyramidal Betz cells is layer V (internal pyramidal layer), found specifically in the primary motor cortex, one layer superficial to the deepest layer.
explanations.D: Correct. The multiform (polymorphic) layer, layer VI, is the deepest layer of the six-layered neocortex, bordering the subcortical white matter, and in most cortical areas is also the broadest layer by thickness, containing a heterogeneous mix of cell shapes whose axons chiefly project to the thalamus. Its position bordering the white matter also makes it the layer most often damaged first in subcortical white-matter disease that spreads toward the cortex.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the multiform (layer VI) as the deepest and broadest layer of the six-layered neocortex.

questions.title: What neuropil excludes
questions.question: which of the following isn't seen in neuropil by electron microscope?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glial (astrocytic and microglial) processes are a normal, expected component of neuropil, contributing to the dense feltwork between cell bodies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This option describes a cell body, but the neuropil-excluded structure the exam is testing is specifically the NEURON cell body; the key names option D, and glial perikarya are likewise outside the neuropil proper but are not the credited answer here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neuronal processes — axons, dendrites, dendritic spines, and axon terminals — are the principal constituents of neuropil, along with synapses formed among them.
explanations.D: Correct. Neuropil is defined as the feltwork of interwoven cell PROCESSES (neuronal and glial) that fills the space between cell bodies (perikarya) in grey matter; by definition, and confirmed on electron microscopy, the cell bodies of neurons are excluded from neuropil, sitting outside it rather than within it. This distinction matters practically because neuropil volume, not neuron number, is what changes most in many degenerative and psychiatric conditions.

questions.learning_objective: State that neuropil comprises neuronal and glial processes, excluding neuronal and glial cell bodies.

questions.title: Climbing fiber synapses
questions.question: One of the following is true about climbing fibres:

options.C: Each fibre synapse with one Purkinje cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. Climbing fibers arise from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, not from the pontine nuclei (which give rise to mossy fibers instead).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Climbing fibers synapse directly on Purkinje cell dendrites, not on granule cells; mossy fibers are the ones that synapse with granule cells in the cerebellar glomeruli.
explanations.C: Correct. Each climbing fiber, arising from the inferior olivary nucleus, forms an unusually powerful, one-to-one synaptic relationship with a single Purkinje cell, wrapping around its dendritic tree and producing a distinctive 'complex spike' — a striking exception to the usual pattern of extensive convergence/divergence seen elsewhere in the cerebellar cortex. This one-to-one wiring is what makes each complex spike such a strong, reliable teaching (error) signal for motor learning.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Climbing fibers are excitatory (glutamatergic), not inhibitory; their powerful excitatory input is exactly what produces the complex spike in the postsynaptic Purkinje cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that each climbing fiber forms a one-to-one synapse with a single Purkinje cell, arising from the inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.title: Muscle spindle structure
questions.question: which of the following is true regarding muscle spindle fibers?

options.A: are important for detection of muscle tension
options.D: they are found in gelatinous fluid filled cavity

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscle spindles detect muscle LENGTH and the rate of change of length (stretch), not tension — tension is instead monitored by the Golgi tendon organ, situated in series with the muscle at the musculotendinous junction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscle spindles carry both sensory innervation (Ia primary and II secondary afferents) and motor innervation (gamma efferents to the intrafusal fibers), so 'only sensory' is incorrect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A typical muscle spindle contains only about two nuclear bag intrafusal fibers (plus several nuclear chain fibers), not six to eight.
explanations.D: Correct. The intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle, along with their sensory and motor nerve endings, sit within a periaxial space filled with a gelatinous fluid inside the spindle's connective-tissue capsule. This fluid-filled compartment cushions the intrafusal fibers and is a distinguishing structural feature separating the spindle from the Golgi tendon organ, which has no comparable capsule.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that muscle spindle intrafusal fibers sit within a gelatinous fluid-filled capsule and carry both sensory and motor innervation.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p5, answer table p10

questions.title: Sensory supply to the angle of the mandible
questions.question: The sensory nerve supply to the skin overlying the angle of the mandible is by the:

options.C: buccal branch of mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve (a dorsal ramus of C2) supplies the posterior scalp, well behind the angle of the mandible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve, a cervical plexus branch, supplies the scalp lateral to the greater occipital nerve's territory and behind the ear, not the angle of the mandible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The buccal branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the skin and mucosa of the cheek anteriorly; trigeminal territory does not extend as far posteroinferiorly as the angle of the mandible.
explanations.D: Correct. The great auricular nerve (C2-C3), a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, ascends over sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and parts of the auricle — cervical-plexus, not trigeminal, territory. A local anaesthetic block of the great auricular nerve is a standard technique for ear and mastoid-area procedures precisely because of this reliable, discrete cutaneous territory.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the great auricular nerve as the cutaneous supply to the skin over the angle of the mandible.

questions.title: Meissner corpuscle description
questions.question: Which of the following is best described as an elongated, encapsulated receptor found in the dermal pegs of glabrous skin and is especially abundant on lips and fingertips?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Merkel's discs are unencapsulated slowly-adapting touch/pressure receptors at the epidermal-dermal junction, not elongated encapsulated structures within dermal pegs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Free nerve endings are unencapsulated, non-specialised endings mediating pain and temperature, not the elongated encapsulated fine-touch receptor described.
explanations.C: Correct. Meissner's corpuscles are elongated, encapsulated, rapidly-adapting fine-touch receptors located within the dermal papillae (pegs) of glabrous (hairless) skin, and are especially concentrated on the fingertips and lips, mediating sensitivity to light touch and texture. This rapid adaptation and high density is exactly what gives fingertips their ability to distinguish fine textures and detect slip during grip.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ruffini's endings are encapsulated but respond to sustained skin stretch/pressure and are found deeper in the dermis, not concentrated in dermal papillae of glabrous skin as Meissner's corpuscles are.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Meissner's corpuscle as the elongated encapsulated fine-touch receptor in dermal papillae of glabrous skin.

questions.title: Retinal layers and the light path
questions.question: Light entering the eye passes through which retinal layer first?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inner nuclear layer (containing bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cell bodies) is crossed after the ganglion cell layer and inner plexiform layer, not first.
explanations.B: Correct. Because the retina is structurally inverted, with photoreceptors at the back against the pigment epithelium, light entering the eye must first cross the innermost retinal layer, the retinal ganglion cell layer, before passing through the inner plexiform, inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers to finally reach the photoreceptors. Despite this seemingly inefficient arrangement, image quality is preserved because these inner layers are thin, transparent and, at the fovea, displaced laterally out of the direct light path.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The outer plexiform layer, where photoreceptors synapse with bipolar and horizontal cells, is crossed near the end of the light path, close to the photoreceptors, not first.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The photoreceptor layer (rods and cones) is the LAST layer light reaches, not the first, precisely because of the retina's inverted architecture.

questions.learning_objective: State that light entering the eye first crosses the retinal ganglion cell layer, given the retina's inverted architecture.

questions.title: Dopamine deficiency in Parkinson disease
questions.question: A wide variety of neurotransmitters have been identified in the cell bodies and afferent synaptic terminals in the basal ganglia. A deficiency of which of the following transmitters is typically associated with Parkinson disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Norepinephrine depletion (locus coeruleus) can occur in Parkinson disease but is not the defining, name-giving neurochemical deficiency.
explanations.B: Correct. Parkinson disease results from progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which normally project to the striatum via the nigrostriatal pathway; the resulting dopamine deficiency underlies the cardinal motor features (bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability) and is the rationale for levodopa therapy. Because the deficiency is presynaptic (loss of the dopamine-producing neurons themselves), replacing the precursor levodopa remains effective even late in disease, unlike disorders where the postsynaptic receptor itself is the problem.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Serotonergic changes can accompany Parkinson disease (contributing to mood symptoms) but are not its defining motor-symptom-causing deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. GABAergic striatal neuron loss is instead the hallmark of Huntington disease, a different basal ganglia disorder with the opposite (hyperkinetic) movement phenotype.

questions.learning_objective: State that Parkinson disease results from dopamine deficiency due to nigrostriatal dopaminergic neuron loss.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p6, answer table p10

questions.title: Saccule macula and vertical linear acceleration
questions.question: Which of the following structures is maximally sensitive to linear head movement in the vertical plane?

options.C: Crista ampullaris of the anterior semicircular duct
options.D: Crista ampullaris of the horizontal semicircular duct

explanations.A: Incorrect. The utricle macula, oriented roughly horizontally, is maximally sensitive to linear acceleration in the horizontal plane (e.g. forward movement, head tilt), not the vertical plane.
explanations.B: Correct. The saccule macula is oriented roughly vertically and is maximally sensitive to linear acceleration in the vertical plane — for example, the sensation of moving in an elevator or standing up. Both maculae achieve this directional sensitivity because their hair-cell stereocilia are embedded in an otolithic membrane weighted with calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia), which lags behind head movement under inertia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The crista ampullaris of the anterior semicircular duct detects angular (rotational) acceleration in its own plane, not linear acceleration in the vertical plane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The crista ampullaris of the horizontal semicircular duct likewise detects angular (rotational), not linear, acceleration.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the saccule macula as maximally sensitive to vertical-plane linear head acceleration, distinct from the horizontal utricle macula.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p6, answer table p10

questions.title: VPM and area 43
questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei is attached to area 43 on cerebral cortex?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus relays touch, proprioceptive and pain/temperature sensation from the BODY and limbs, projecting to the body's somatosensory cortex representation, not the face-associated area 43.
explanations.B: Correct. The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays sensation (including taste) from the face and oral cavity, projecting to the face representation of the somatosensory cortex near area 43 (the gustatory/opercular-insular region). This VPL/VPM split mirrors the body/face split already familiar from the spinal trigeminal versus dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathways further downstream.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The medial thalamic nuclear group is chiefly involved in limbic and associative functions, not somatosensory relay to area 43.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ventrolateral thalamic group relays motor (cerebellar and basal ganglia) information to the motor cortex, not sensory information to area 43.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the VPM as the thalamic relay for facial sensation to the cortical face representation near area 43.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p6, answer table p10

questions.title: Bilateral corticobulbar innervation
questions.question: Which of the following sentence is true regarding descending motor tracts?

options.A: fine movements are mainly controlled by ventral corticospinal tract
options.B: there is delay in the pyramidal tract impulses
options.D: corticobulbar tract is bilaterally innervated to all cranial nucleus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fine, discrete movements (e.g. of the digits) are chiefly mediated by the crossed lateral corticospinal tract, which is by far the larger of the two corticospinal divisions; the small ventral corticospinal tract instead mainly controls axial/postural musculature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pyramidal (corticospinal) tract is a fast, largely direct pathway with minimal synaptic delay, which is part of why pyramidal lesions produce such immediate motor deficits.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While motor development is broadly cephalocaudal and proximodistal (gross motor skills like standing do precede fine motor skills like writing), this is a developmental observation rather than a statement about the organisation of a descending tract, and it is not the option credited by the printed key.
explanations.D: Correct. As a general organising rule, the corticobulbar tract supplies most cranial nerve motor nuclei bilaterally, from both cerebral hemispheres, which is why a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion typically spares most cranial-nerve-supplied muscles; the lower facial nucleus and the hypoglossal nucleus's genioglossus-supplying part are the important clinical exceptions, receiving predominantly contralateral input. This is the physiological basis for the classic bedside sign of a central (upper motor neuron) facial palsy sparing the forehead, versus a peripheral (lower motor neuron, CN VII) palsy that does not.

questions.learning_objective: State the general rule that the corticobulbar tract supplies cranial nerve motor nuclei bilaterally.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p6, answer table p10

questions.title: Cerebellar somatotopy
questions.question: Which structures in the cerebellum have a topographical representation of the body?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dentate nucleus, the largest and most lateral deep cerebellar nucleus, is an OUTPUT relay for the lateral hemispheres (neocerebellum) and does not itself carry a somatotopic body map.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral hemispheres (neocerebellum/cerebrocerebellum) process cortically-relayed information for planning and coordinating skilled voluntary movement, without a direct somatotopic body map comparable to the vermis/intermediate zone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The flocculonodular lobe (archicerebellum/vestibulocerebellum) is concerned with balance and eye movement coordination via vestibular connections, not with a topographic body map.
explanations.D: Correct. The vermis and the flanking intermediate (paravermal) zone together form the spinocerebellum, which receives somatotopically organised proprioceptive input from the spinal cord and so carries a topographical representation of the body (trunk medially near the vermis, limbs more laterally in the intermediate zone). This organisation is why a lesion confined to the vermis produces truncal/gait ataxia, while a more lateral intermediate-zone lesion instead produces limb ataxia on the same side.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the vermis and intermediate zone as the cerebellar regions carrying a topographical body map.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 1, p7, answer table p10

questions.title: Ventromedial hypothalamic lesion syndrome
questions.question: Bilateral lesions involving the ventromedial hypothalamus will lead to which of the following deficits?

options.C: Excessive eating, rage and aggression, hyperactivity

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decreased eating and drinking is instead the effect of a LATERAL hypothalamic (feeding centre) lesion, the opposite syndrome to a ventromedial lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Loss of sexual drive is more classically linked to other hypothalamic or limbic lesions, not the defining feature of an isolated ventromedial lesion.
explanations.C: Correct. The ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus normally acts as a satiety centre, restraining feeding once caloric needs are met, and also modulates aggressive behaviour; bilateral destruction removes this restraint, producing hyperphagia (leading to obesity), increased rage, aggression, and hyperactivity. This is the mirror image of the lateral hypothalamic (feeding centre) lesion syndrome, which instead causes aphagia and adipsia, reflecting the two nuclei's reciprocal roles in energy balance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Obsessive-compulsive features localise to different circuits (notably orbitofrontal-striatal-thalamic loops), not to the ventromedial hypothalamic satiety centre.

questions.learning_objective: State the ventromedial hypothalamic lesion syndrome of hyperphagia, obesity, rage and aggression.

questions.title: The crossed extensor reflex
questions.question: Which of the following reflexes best describes incoming pain signals that elicit movements performed by antagonistic muscle groups on either side of the body?

explanations.A: Correct. The crossed extensor reflex is the polysynaptic spinal reflex in which a painful stimulus produces ipsilateral flexor withdrawal together with, via cord-crossing interneurons, contralateral extensor activation — antagonistic movements (flexion vs extension) occurring on opposite sides of the body simultaneously. Functionally this reflex lets the body immediately redistribute weight onto the unharmed limb the instant the injured limb is withdrawn, preserving balance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The withdrawal reflex alone describes only the ipsilateral flexion response to a painful stimulus, without the contralateral, opposite-side component the question specifically asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reciprocal inhibition describes relaxation of an antagonist muscle at ONE joint on one side, not a bilateral, cord-crossing reflex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Autogenic inhibition is the Golgi tendon organ-mediated relaxation of the SAME muscle under excessive tension, unrelated to a painful stimulus eliciting opposite-side movement.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the crossed extensor reflex as contralateral limb extension accompanying ipsilateral withdrawal from pain.

questions.title: Face representation in the motor homunculus
questions.question: Which of the following body parts is represented most laterally and inferiorly within the primary motor cortex?

explanations.A: Correct. In the inverted somatotopic homunculus of the primary motor cortex, the face, lips and tongue — which require the finest, most differentiated motor control — are represented most laterally and inferiorly, near the lateral (Sylvian) fissure, occupying a disproportionately large cortical territory. This exaggeration of cortical territory relative to actual body-part size is exactly what the classic motor homunculus cartoon (with its huge lips and hands) is drawn to illustrate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hand occupies a large, disproportionate territory in the motor homunculus, but sits at the mid-convexity, not as laterally/inferiorly as the face representation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lower limb is represented superiorly on the motor cortex, extending onto the medial surface of the hemisphere (paracentral lobule) — the opposite end of the homunculus from the face.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The abdomen/trunk occupies a mid-convexity position between the limb representations, not the most lateral/inferior position.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the face representation as the most lateral and inferior part of the primary motor cortex homunculus.

questions.title: Superior olivary nucleus and sound localization
questions.question: Which brainstem structure plays a major role in determining the direction from which a sound originates?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cochlear nucleus is the first central relay for auditory input from one ear, but it has not yet combined information from both ears, so it cannot itself localise sound direction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior colliculus is an important auditory midbrain relay and integration centre, but the FIRST binaural convergence for localisation happens more caudally, at the superior olivary complex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior olivary nucleus is an unrelated medullary structure that gives rise to cerebellar climbing fibers; despite the similar name, it plays no role in auditory sound localisation.
explanations.D: Correct. The superior olivary complex, in the caudal pons, is the first site in the ascending auditory pathway where inputs from both cochlear nuclei converge on the same neurons, allowing it to compute interaural time differences and interaural intensity differences and so determine the direction a sound is coming from. Interaural time differences are most useful for localising low-frequency sounds, while interaural intensity differences dominate for high-frequency sounds, since the head casts more of a sound 'shadow' at higher frequencies.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superior olivary nucleus as the brainstem site of binaural convergence for sound localization.

questions.title: Retinal ganglion cells and action potentials
questions.question: Which of the following retinal cells have action potentials?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Photoreceptors signal by graded (analogue) membrane potential changes in response to light, not by firing action potentials.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bipolar cells likewise relay information via graded potentials over the short distance to the inner plexiform layer, without firing true spikes.
explanations.C: Correct. Retinal ganglion cells integrate graded input from the inner retina and are the retina's exception: they generate true, all-or-none action potentials, which then propagate the length of the optic nerve axon to the brain. Spiking is necessary here specifically because the optic nerve axon must carry the signal a long distance without the decrement a purely graded potential would suffer over that length.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Horizontal cells, like the other interneurons of the outer retina, modulate signalling laterally through graded potentials rather than action potentials.

questions.learning_objective: State that retinal ganglion cells, not photoreceptors, bipolar or horizontal cells, generate action potentials.

questions.title: Strychnine and glycine receptors
questions.question: Which of the following structure is inhibited by strychnine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glutamate is the CNS's principal excitatory transmitter and is not the target strychnine antagonises; strychnine acts on an inhibitory system instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GABA-A receptors are instead the target potentiated by barbiturates and benzodiazepines, not the receptor strychnine blocks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histamine is a wakefulness-promoting neurotransmitter unrelated to strychnine's mechanism.
explanations.D: Correct. Strychnine is a competitive antagonist at glycine receptors; because glycine is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of spinal interneurons (notably Renshaw cells), blocking it removes spinal inhibition and produces uncontrolled motor neuron excitation, manifesting as severe muscle spasms and convulsions. Historically, strychnine poisoning was a recognised cause of death by asphyxiation from sustained spasm of the respiratory muscles, which is why the drug is no longer used therapeutically.

questions.learning_objective: State that strychnine produces convulsions by antagonising the inhibitory neurotransmitter glycine.

questions.title: Barbiturates and GABA potentiation
questions.question: barbiturates potentiate the effect of which of the following substance?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glutamate is excitatory; barbiturates potentiate an INHIBITORY system, not glutamatergic excitation.
explanations.B: Correct. Barbiturates bind an allosteric site on the GABA-A receptor and potentiate its action by prolonging the duration the chloride channel stays open in the presence of GABA, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission. At higher concentrations they can also open the channel directly, underlying both their sedative-anticonvulsant efficacy and their narrow, dangerous therapeutic index. This direct, GABA-independent channel-opening at high dose is exactly why barbiturate overdose causes fatal respiratory depression in a way pure benzodiazepine overdose usually does not.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histamine is unrelated to the chloride-channel mechanism barbiturates act through.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glycine is potentiated by different agents (e.g. some anaesthetics); barbiturates' defining potentiation target in this context is GABA, not glycine.

questions.learning_objective: State that barbiturates potentiate GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition by prolonging chloride channel opening.

questions.title: The phrenic nucleus is cervical, not thoracic
questions.question: which of the following nucleus isn't found in thoracic segment of spinal cord?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The intermediolateral (sympathetic) nucleus of the lateral horn is a genuinely thoracic (and upper lumbar, T1-L2) structure, the origin of preganglionic sympathetic outflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nucleus proprius, the main relay nucleus of the dorsal horn, is present throughout the spinal cord including thoracic segments.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Clark's (dorsal) nucleus, present at T1-L2, gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract and is a genuinely thoracic structure.
explanations.D: Correct. The phrenic nucleus, which gives rise to the phrenic nerve supplying the diaphragm, is located in the CERVICAL spinal cord (chiefly C3-C5), not in any thoracic segment — the diaphragm's motor nucleus is cervical even though the muscle it innervates lies in the thorax/abdomen. This is the anatomical basis of the mnemonic 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive,' and of why a high cervical cord injury above C3 is immediately fatal without ventilatory support.

questions.subtopic: Thoracic spinal cord grey matter nuclei
questions.learning_objective: State that the phrenic nucleus is cervical (C3-C5), not thoracic, unlike the nucleus proprius, Clark's nucleus and the sympathetic nucleus.

questions.title: Superior sagittal sinus in the falx cerebri
questions.question: What is the origin of the structure passes in this groove?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior sagittal sinus runs in the FREE inferior border of the falx cerebri, not the groove shown, and drains into the straight sinus rather than the confluence of sinuses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The straight sinus runs along the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, a different groove from the one at the superior attached border of the falx.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sigmoid sinus is an S-shaped continuation of the transverse sinus running toward the jugular foramen, unrelated to the falx cerebri groove shown.
explanations.D: Correct. The superior sagittal sinus runs within the superior, attached border of the falx cerebri, from the crista galli anteriorly to the internal occipital protuberance posteriorly, where it typically becomes the right transverse sinus at the confluence of sinuses. Along its course it also receives the superior cerebral veins and drains arachnoid granulations, making it central to both venous drainage and CSF absorption.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the superior sagittal sinus within the attached superior border of the falx cerebri.

questions.title: Cuneate nucleus as second-order neuron for the finger
questions.question: What is the second order neuron of this tract starts from the finger?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The substantia gelatinosa of Rolando is a dorsal horn region involved in modulating pain transmission, not the second-order relay of the dorsal column pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Clark's (dorsal) nucleus gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, an UNCONSCIOUS proprioceptive pathway, not the conscious dorsal column pathway the finger's fine touch/proprioception travels in.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The gracile nucleus is the second-order neuron for the LOWER limb and lower trunk, reached via the fasciculus gracilis, not for the finger/upper limb.
explanations.D: Correct. Fibers carrying fine touch and conscious proprioception from the upper limb, including the finger, ascend in the fasciculus cuneatus and synapse on their second-order neuron in the cuneate nucleus of the lower medulla, whose fibers then decussate as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. This decussation in the medulla, rather than in the spinal cord, is why a single medullary lesion can produce a distinctive pattern of contralateral fine touch/proprioceptive loss alongside other crossed or uncrossed brainstem signs.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cuneate nucleus as the second-order neuron for conscious proprioceptive/fine touch input from the finger and upper limb.

questions.title: Hypoglossal nerve in the preolivary sulcus
questions.question: Tumour in the structure shown by the red arrow will lead to loss of which of the following structure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vagus nerve rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus, behind the olive, a different groove from the one shown (between pyramid and olive).
explanations.B: Correct. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) rootlets emerge in the anterolateral (preolivary) sulcus, the groove between the medullary pyramid and the olive; a mass lesion compressing this groove characteristically damages the hypoglossal rootlets, producing ipsilateral tongue weakness and deviation toward the lesion on protrusion. This 'tongue points to the side of the lesion' sign is a classic bedside finding used to localise a lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sublingual gland is a peripheral structure supplied indirectly via the facial nerve/chorda tympani pathway, unrelated to this specific medullary groove.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like the vagus, the glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus behind the olive, not the preolivary groove shown.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the hypoglossal nerve rootlets in the preolivary sulcus and link compression there to hypoglossal deficits.

questions.title: Spinothalamic tract termination in the VPL
questions.question: What is the termination of tracts starts at receptors referred by red arrow?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The VPM is reserved for the trigeminothalamic (facial) pain/sensory pathway; body-receptor spinothalamic fibers instead terminate in the VPL.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The insular cortex is a higher-order pain-processing area reached later in the pathway, not the thalamic relay nucleus itself where these second-order fibers first terminate.
explanations.C: Correct. The anterolateral (spinothalamic) system carrying pain, temperature and crude touch from body (limb/trunk) receptors has its second-order neurons decussate near the level of entry and ascend to terminate in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus, which then relays onward to the postcentral gyrus. Because these second-order fibers decussate near their level of entry, a spinal cord hemisection produces contralateral (not ipsilateral) loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, the key finding in Brown-Séquard syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortex) is the THIRD-order (cortical) destination, reached after the thalamic VPL relay, not the tract's direct thalamic termination point being asked about.

questions.learning_objective: State that spinothalamic fibers carrying sensation from body receptors terminate in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus.
